title: Reverse Linked List II
directAnswer: Use a dummy node before the head so the case 'left = 1' needs no special handling. Walk a pointer to the node just before position left, then reverse only the sublist from left to right. Two clean ways: (1) reverse the sublist in place with the prev/curr flip and reconnect the three boundary links, or (2) the one-pass head-insertion trick — repeatedly pull the node after curr to the front of the sublist. Both are O(n) time, O(1) space, single traversal.

remember.pattern: Dummy node + bounded in-place sublist reversal
remember.formula:
dummy -> head; prevLeft = dummy
advance prevLeft (left-1) times
# head-insertion, repeat (right-left) times:
curr = prevLeft.next
for _ in range(right - left):
    nxt = curr.next
    curr.next = nxt.next
    nxt.next = prevLeft.next
    prevLeft.next = nxt
return dummy.next
rules: Use a **dummy node** in front of `head` so reversing from position 1 (`left = 1`) isn't a special case.
Stop the leading walk at the node **just before** `left` (`prevLeft`) — you need it to re-link the reversed head.
Positions are **1-indexed** and the range `[left, right]` is **inclusive**.
Re-link **three** boundaries: prevLeft → new sub-head, old sub-head (now sub-tail) → the node after `right`.
It's a **single pass** in O(1) space — no second traversal and no extra list.
whenToUse: Reverse only a contiguous segment of a singly linked list
Any in-place pointer rewrite bounded by two positions
Problems that reverse a window then stitch it back (k-group, partial reversals)
When a dummy node simplifies head-adjacent edge cases
antiSignals: You must reverse the WHOLE list → plain Reverse Linked List (no boundaries)
Reverse in fixed-size blocks repeatedly → Reverse Nodes in k-Group
You may not mutate the input → build a new list instead of rewiring pointers
remember.takeaway: Reverse Linked List II is the partial-reversal workhorse: a dummy node erases the head edge case, and the only real subtlety is reconnecting the three boundary links. Master the head-insertion one-pass here and Reverse Nodes in k-Group becomes a short step away.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can reverse a bounded segment in place without losing the rest of the list, handle 1-indexing and the inclusive range, and reconnect the boundary pointers correctly — especially the edge case left = 1.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Off-by-one on the walk to prevLeft, forgetting the dummy so left = 1 breaks, or mis-stitching the boundaries (leaving a gap or a cycle between the reversed segment and the tail).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Use a dummy node, show the one-pass head-insertion method, and articulate exactly which three links get rewired and why the original sub-head becomes the sub-tail that must point to the node after right.

problemStatement:
Given the `head` of a singly linked list and two integers `left` and `right` where `left <= right`, reverse the nodes of the list from position `left` to position `right`, and return *the reversed list*.

Positions are 1-indexed: the head is position 1. The reversal is over the **inclusive** range `[left, right]`.
constraints: The number of nodes in the list is n
Follow up: can you do it in one pass?
understanding: We reverse only the contiguous segment between 1-indexed positions left and right, leaving the prefix and suffix untouched, and splice the reversed segment back in. No nodes are created and no values copied — only next pointers change. When left == right the list is unchanged.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the positions 1-indexed, and is the range inclusive?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — position 1 is the head, and [left, right] is inclusive. So left=2, right=4 reverses the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th nodes.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can left equal 1 (reversing from the head)?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, and that's the tricky case because the head itself changes. A dummy node in front of head removes the special-casing entirely.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I mutate the nodes, and is one pass required?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: In-place mutation is expected and gives O(1) space. The follow-up asks for one pass, which the head-insertion method achieves.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if left == right?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Then there's a single node in the range and nothing to reverse — return the list unchanged. My loop runs zero times in that case.

examples.explanation: The segment 2→3→4 is reversed to 4→3→2; node 1 (prefix) and node 5 (suffix) stay put.
Single node, left == right — nothing to reverse.
Reversing from position 1 changes the head — the dummy node makes this seamless.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: A dummy node plus a bounded reversal; head-insertion is the elegant one-pass variant.

approaches.name: Reverse the Sublist In Place, Then Reconnect
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this — it's the most intuitive. Phrase it as 'reverse just the [left, right] window with the standard flip, then stitch the three boundary links'.
hints: Add a dummy node before head so reversing from position 1 isn't special. Walk a pointer to the node just before position left and remember it.
From there, run the ordinary prev/curr/next reversal, but only for the (right - left + 1) nodes in the window.

After reversing, you have three loose ends: the node before left, the new head of the reversed window (old position right), and the new tail (old position left) which must point to whatever followed right.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One walk to position left (≤ n steps) plus one reversal pass over the window (≤ n steps) — a single overall traversal, so O(n) time. Only a constant number of pointers are used, so O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
This approach reuses the muscle memory from full-list reversal and confines it to a window.

**The dummy node erases the head edge case.** When `left = 1`, the reversal changes the list's head, which would otherwise require special handling. Prepending a `dummy` node whose `next` is `head` means the 'node before the window' always exists — even when the window starts at position 1, the node before it is simply the dummy. We return `dummy.next` at the end, which is the (possibly new) real head.

**Find the anchor, then reverse the window.** We walk `beforeLeft` forward `left - 1` steps so it sits on the node immediately before position `left`. The window to reverse is then `beforeLeft.next` through the node at position `right`. We apply the classic three-pointer flip — `prev`, `curr`, `next` — but only `right - left + 1` times, so it stops exactly at the window's end. When the loop finishes, `prev` points at the node that was at position `right` (the window's new head), and `curr` points at the node just past `right` (the start of the untouched suffix).

**Reconnecting the three boundaries is the whole game.** Reversing the window in isolation leaves it detached. Three links restore the list:

1. The node that *was* first in the window (position `left`) is now its **tail**. We captured it as `subTail = beforeLeft.next` *before* rewiring, because `beforeLeft.next` still points there.
2. `beforeLeft.next = prev` splices the prefix onto the window's new head (old `right`).
3. `subTail.next = curr` connects the window's new tail to the suffix (the node after old `right`).

Get any of those three wrong and you either drop the suffix, leave a gap, or create a cycle. Naming them explicitly — 'prefix → new head, new tail → suffix' — is what keeps the wiring straight under pressure.

**Why capture subTail early.** The original first node of the window becomes the tail after reversal, but its identity is easiest to grab *before* the reversal mutates pointers: it's exactly `beforeLeft.next` at the moment we arrive. Stash it, then reverse, then use it to attach the suffix.
approaches.insight: A bounded reversal is just the ordinary reversal with a step counter, sandwiched between two pointer hand-offs. The dummy node neutralizes the head case, and the only genuinely new idea versus full reversal is that the *first* node of the window becomes the node you must reattach to the suffix.

dryRun.intro: Dummy → 1. Walk beforeLeft to node 1 (left-1=1 step). Reverse 3 nodes [2,3,4], then reconnect.

code.python:
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next

def reverseBetween(self, head: ListNode, left: int, right: int) -> ListNode:
    if head is None or left == right:
        return head
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    before_left = dummy
    for _ in range(left - 1):
        before_left = before_left.next
    sub_tail = before_left.next  # old position left -> becomes the tail
    prev = None
    curr = before_left.next
    for _ in range(right - left + 1):
        nxt = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = nxt
    before_left.next = prev   # prefix -> new head (old position right)
    sub_tail.next = curr      # new tail -> suffix (node after right)
    return dummy.next

approaches.name: Head-Insertion — True One Pass
approaches.whenToMention: Offer for the explicit 'one pass' follow-up. Repeatedly move the node after curr to the front of the window — no separate reversal phase.
hints: Keep curr fixed on the window's first node. Each step, take the node right after curr and splice it to the front of the window (just after prevLeft).
Doing that (right - left) times slides every later window node ahead of curr, which naturally leaves curr at the back — the window is reversed.
Three pointer assignments per step: detach curr.next, point it at prevLeft.next, then make it the new prevLeft.next.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single walk to prevLeft plus right - left splice operations, each O(1). One overall traversal → O(n) time, O(1) space with a constant number of pointers.
approaches.explanation:
Head-insertion reverses the window without ever building it in isolation — it threads each node to the front as it goes, so the list stays connected the whole time.

**The fixed anchor and the fixed curr.** `prevLeft` sits just before the window (again, the dummy guarantees it exists). `curr` is pinned to the window's *first* node and never moves forward — instead, the nodes behind it get pulled ahead of it. Because `curr` ends up at the back of the window, it naturally becomes the reversed segment's tail.

**One splice per step.** On each iteration we grab `nxt = curr.next`, the node immediately after `curr`. Three assignments relocate it to the front of the window:

1. `curr.next = nxt.next` — unhook `nxt`, so `curr` now skips over it.
2. `nxt.next = prevLeft.next` — point `nxt` at the current front of the window.
3. `prevLeft.next = nxt` — make `nxt` the new front.

After this, `nxt` has jumped to the head of the window and everything else shifted back by one. Repeating `right - left` times pulls every later window node in front of `curr`, fully reversing the segment.

**Why it's genuinely one pass.** There's no 'reverse then reconnect' split: the boundary links are maintained continuously by the three assignments. `prevLeft.next` always points at the current window head, and `curr.next` always points at the suffix, so the list is valid after every step. That continuous correctness is what makes head-insertion the canonical answer to the 'can you do it in one pass?' follow-up.

**The order of the three lines is fixed.** Detach before you redirect, redirect before you re-anchor. Swap any two and you either lose `nxt.next` or strand part of the window — the same discipline as the classic three-pointer flip, just applied to relocation instead of in-place reversal.
approaches.insight: Head-insertion reframes 'reverse a window' as 'repeatedly move the second window node to the front'. Keeping curr stationary and sliding others past it means the list never breaks apart, so there's nothing to reconnect at the end — the elegance interviewers reward on the one-pass follow-up.

code.python:
def reverseBetween(self, head: ListNode, left: int, right: int) -> ListNode:
    if head is None or left == right:
        return head
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    prev_left = dummy
    for _ in range(left - 1):
        prev_left = prev_left.next
    curr = prev_left.next  # stays put; later nodes move ahead of it
    for _ in range(right - left):
        nxt = curr.next
        curr.next = nxt.next       # detach nxt
        nxt.next = prev_left.next  # nxt points at current window head
        prev_left.next = nxt       # nxt becomes the new window head
    return dummy.next

java.explanation: Anchor that always sits just before the window — dummy handles left = 1.
The window's first node; it stays fixed and ends up as the window's tail.
The node to relocate to the front of the window this step.
Detach nxt by linking curr past it.
Point nxt at the current window head.
Make nxt the new window head — the list stays connected throughout.

Splice nxt to the front of the window.
nxt is the new head; no end-of-loop reconnection needed.

edgeCases.behavior: prevLeft is the dummy; the new head emerges as dummy.next, returned correctly.
Loop runs zero times; list unchanged.
One splice swaps them; list stays valid throughout.

pitfalls: Reordering the three splice lines — detach, then redirect, then re-anchor.
Looping right - left + 1 times instead of right - left (over-rotates the window).
Advancing curr each iteration — curr must stay fixed as the window's first node.
Skipping the dummy and special-casing left = 1.

commonMistakes: Not using a dummy node, forcing a special case when left = 1.
Off-by-one walking to the node before left (1-indexing).
Mis-stitching the boundaries — dropping the suffix, leaving a gap, or creating a cycle.
Reversing the wrong number of nodes (right - left vs right - left + 1 confusion).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Skipping the dummy node
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When left = 1 the head itself changes. Without a dummy you must branch on 'is left 1?' and reattach the head manually — error-prone. A dummy makes 'the node before the window' always exist.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting to capture the sublist tail
commonMistakesDetailed.why: In the reverse-then-reconnect method, the window's first node becomes its tail and must point to the suffix. If you don't capture it before reversing, beforeLeft.next no longer points to it and the suffix is lost.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
prev = None
curr = before_left.next
for _ in range(right - left + 1):
    nxt = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = nxt
before_left.next = prev
# forgot to connect the old sub-head to the suffix -> tail dangles
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
sub_tail = before_left.next   # capture BEFORE reversing
prev = None
curr = before_left.next
for _ in range(right - left + 1):
    nxt = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = nxt
before_left.next = prev
sub_tail.next = curr          # reattach the suffix

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong iteration count on the window
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The inclusive range [left, right] has right - left + 1 nodes. The reverse-then-reconnect flip runs that many times; the head-insertion method runs right - left times (one fewer, since curr stays put). Mixing them up over- or under-reverses.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
# head-insertion but looping one too many times
for _ in range(right - left + 1):
    nxt = curr.next
    curr.next = nxt.next; nxt.next = prev_left.next; prev_left.next = nxt
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
# head-insertion: exactly right - left splices
for _ in range(right - left):
    nxt = curr.next
    curr.next = nxt.next; nxt.next = prev_left.next; prev_left.next = nxt
